{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals a consistent pattern of German legal organizations, specifically courts (Bundesfinanzgericht, Verwaltungsgerichtshof), tax authorities (Finanzamt, Magistrat), and companies (GmbH). The primary challenge is distinguishing these from common nouns or other capitalized words, which is solved by anchoring to specific legal context verbs (hat, gegen, vom) and prepositions (des, an den).",
  "strategy": "Use 5 targeted regex rules anchored by specific legal context keywords (e.g., 'Das', 'des', 'an den') to capture the organization names that follow, ensuring high precision by avoiding generic capitalization rules.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use lookbehind or context anchors to ensure the match is an organization in a legal context.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "Courts (Bundesfinanzgericht/Verwaltungsgerichtshof)",
      "description": "Matches specific court names following 'Das' or 'des' or 'an den'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?<=\\b(Das|des|an\\s+den)\\s+)(Bundesfinanzgericht(?:es)?(?:\\s*\\(BFG\\))?|Verwaltungsgerichtshof(?:es)?)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "High frequency courts are almost always preceded by specific articles/prepositions in this text type. The pattern captures the full name including optional suffixes like '(BFG)' or genitive 'es'."
    },
    {
      "name": "Tax Authorities (Finanzamt/Magistrat)",
      "description": "Matches Finanzamt or Magistrat der Stadt Wien following 'des', 'vom', 'an den', or 'durch'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?<=\\b(des|vom|an\\s+den|durch)\\s+)(Finanzamt(?:es)?(?:\\s+Österreich)?|Magistrat(?:s?)\\s+der\\s+Stadt\\s+Wien)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Tax authorities are frequently mentioned as the subject or object of a decision. The pattern handles variations like 'Finanzamt', 'Finanzamtes', and the full 'Magistrat der Stadt Wien'."
    },
    {
      "name": "Companies (GmbH)",
      "description": "Matches company names ending in GmbH following 'der' or 'der ... GmbH'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?<=\\bder\\s+)([A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9\\-]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9\\-]+)*\\s+GmbH)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Companies are identified by the suffix 'GmbH'. The lookbehind 'der' ensures it's a possessive context (e.g., 'der Fenbruck-Pharma GmbH') rather than a random capitalized word."
    },
    {
      "name": "Abbreviations (BFG)",
      "description": "Matches the abbreviation BFG when used as a standalone noun in legal context.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?<=\\b(für\\s+das|an\\s+das|vom|des)\\s+)(BFG)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "'BFG' appears as an abbreviation for Bundesfinanzgericht. It needs context to distinguish it from other acronyms."
    },
    {
      "name": "Specific Tax Office (FA)",
      "description": "Matches specific tax office names like 'FA Schwechat Gerasdorf'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?<=\\bdes\\s+)(FA\\s+[A-Z][a-zA-Z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zA-Z]+)?)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "'FA' is a specific abbreviation for Finanzamt followed by a location. The pattern captures the full specific name."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

        "type": "organisation"

    },
    {
      "name": "Corporate entities (GmbH)",
      "description": "Matches companies ending in GmbH.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b([A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9\\-]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-zA-Z0-9\\-]+)*\\s+GmbH)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "Captures private companies which are frequent entities in tax disputes."
    },
    {
      "name": "Federal Ministers/Departments",
      "description": "Matches specific federal ministries mentioned in legal contexts.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "\\b(Bundesminister(?:in)? für [A-Za-z, ]+|Bundesamt für [A-Za-z ]+)\\b",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "organisation"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 4,
      "reasoning": "Captures specific government bodies like the Federal Ministry of Labour."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []

- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

IMPORTANT:
- Do NOT assume entities are capitalized; check the training data.
- Prefer structural patterns (\d+, [A-Z][a-z]+) over memorized alternations.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.

- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
